#3909. Cyberpunk 2077 mod Torrent adds 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City

A new Cyberpunk 2077 mod has overhauled Night City's rain, swapping the game's flat wet weather effects for individual 3D drops and adding lightning storms.

As spotted by DSOGaming, modder CyanideX's mod, Torrent, gives each raindrop its own size and falling speed. The drops also react to the player's movement, so they stream towards the windscreen when you're driving fast. If you find the wind has picked up, blustery weather can also push them sideways, too.

The rain also catches the light from street lamps, neon signs, car headlights, and taillights, and won't fall through roofs or inside buildings. Drops splash on the ground, heavy rain leaves mist in the distance, and cars throw up spray from their tyres on wet roads.

The mod complements this with a new lightning system, with branching bolts that flash and flicker before fading, and that can arrive in bursts during heavier storms.

If you like a little lightning, the frequency of bolts can be adjusted across 10 levels, and with the AudioXL mod installed, thunder follows each strike, timed to how far away it landed.

For players sensitive to flashing lights, a Reduce Flashes option dims the lightning, replaces its flicker with a single slow glow, and halves the number of strikes.

Torrent supports Nova City 2 and other weather mods, and adds extra storm effects for Nova City 2 players, including mist that rolls through the streets with the wind. It’s available now on Nexus Mods.

Niko Bellic is one of my favorite GTA protagonists, a down-to-earth immigrant looking for a better life in Liberty City, though admittedly with a few anger issues and skeletons in his closet.

Still, when people spotted that Niko's voice actor, Michael Hollick, was listed in the GTA 6 credits as "The Hitman", the rumour mill really kicked into overdrive around whether he was playing the same character.

Everyone knows how much GTA games love their callbacks and cameos, though I'm sure no one would want him to meet the same fate as Johnny from the Lost and Damned in GTA 5. Again, if you don't want to know who Hollick plays in GTA 6, then leave now.

The straight answer is, yes, Niko does appear in GTA 6 during Chapter 5: Top of the World, Ma, near the very end of the game, specifically, in the Taking Liberties mission. Obviously, he's a lot older and more grizzled considering GTA 4 was released *checks watch* 18 years ago (I immediately turned to dust).

I won't go into the specifics of his appearance—you can definitely track it down if you want to, but you've most likely still got quite a few Chapters to play through before you'll reach this cameo. It's definitely a fun one for us fans of Niko and who still think the 4th game in the series is the best, though GTA 6 might convince me yet.

#3907. Rasen, out in early access now, is a PvP focused take on Dark Souls that borrows one of fighting games' best techy tricks

The idea of Dark Souls PvP has always scared me a tad. You can replace Dark Souls with Bloodborne or Elden Ring, I've typically just been a coward when it comes to the idea of fighting another, real person. They're probably going to be better than me! I don't use tactics in Souls games, I use brute force until I get my way! That being said, I do have to admit I quite like the look of Rasen, a game that is essentially just the PvP component of Dark Souls (or PvE if you just want to take on some computer-controlled enemies) that just launched into early access.

To say that it is just straight up Dark Souls combat would be unfair, from the looks of things. For one, it looks more like it leans a tad towards Sekiro with a blades-only kind of affair, whether that be big or small. And blades a plenty they have, ranging from your classic sword, to scythes, to halberds and all sorts. It's a much flashier looking affair too, with fancy slashing effects that seem to buff moves and a pace that seems much faster than Souls games tend to be.

You can take part in matches with up to eight people, which presumably extends to AI (not that kind) enemies too, in "atmospheric duels, clashes, deathmatches and more." It looks neat! And best of all, unusually for a 3D arena fighter, it has rollback netcode. For those unfamiliar, and to try and explain it simply, this is essentially a bit of tech you'll find in predominantly 2D fighting games that predicts every possible input you could make in a given moment, helping to reduce lag time and allow for tighter matches (and less rage quitting).

That's a bit harder to do in a 3D environment given that you have a lot more options at your disposal when it comes to movement, so if it works that's some impressive stuff! And we could all quite easily find out together, as a demo for Rasen is available to try out. Or, alternatively, you can just pick it up whole hog on Steam right now, as it's available in early access.

#3906. Forage and fight for ingredients in a magical 1960s Italy and whip up some tasty meals Cooking Mama style in The Snackbar at the End of the World

If a game is about cooking, at minimum I'll have to give it a quick testspin. Outside of this whole writing about video games thing, my other lot in life is soul bound to food, so I'm always curious to see how the two can be mixed together. And earlier this week, The Snackbar at the End of the World was revealed, a wonderfully cartoonish action-adventure game set in a magical, slightly post-apocalyptic version of 1960s Italy where you go out and forage for ingredients while fending off monstrous crops before turning them into tasty meals back in your struggling restaurant.

First up, I just have to gush over the artstyle a bit. The whole game is hand-drawn with a colourful, comic book look that has an impressive sense of depth to it. It gives off a deep love of Italian architecture and landscapes, and that admiration clearly extends to the food too. Once you've gotten the ingredients you need, you then, loosely in the vein of Cooking Mama, prepare them and make various classic Italian dishes by performing some quick minigames. Simple, but charming! The rest of the time you're off killing some ghoulies that look like mutated fruit and veggies, with the occasional fungus-possessed hog and, uh, haunted statues? I think?

I'm also quite pleased about two points made on the game's Steam page. First is the content description: "This game features cartoon violence, sensitive political themes set in a fictional world, and depictions of an oppressive government committing crimes against its citizens." There is clearly a romantic quality to the game and I'd be worried if it didn't acknowledge any of the political context of the decades preceding.

The other line reads, "Every sound effect, musical note, design decision, and line of code is human-made. Because this game is about human relationships and delicious food – and that’s not a story we would ever trust AI to tell." Thank the lord! Right now there's no release date attached to The Snackbar at the End of the World, unsurprising given it was only announced this week. But while we all wait for a date, you could perhaps join me in throwing it a wishlist on Steam.

#3905. Police arrest suspect after drive-by shooting at office campus housing Xbox studio inXile

Police are still investigating the motive.

Police have arrested a suspect after a drive-by shooting at an office campus in Tustin, California, which is home to Xbox-owned studio inXile Entertainment.

According to Aftermath, officers responded to reports of a drive-by shooting at Flight at Tustin Legacy, a campus that houses inXile and other businesses, on 11th November.

"Located multiple shell casings. Nobody was hurt," Tustin Police Sergeant Christopher Peterson told the outlet. "Processed the crime scene, and then sometime [Friday] morning, a little before 11 [AM], they took a suspect into custody. And the investigation is still kind of ongoing as to where and why."

"We're relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," an inXile spokesperson said. "Our focus is on supporting our team, and we are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate."

Police have not given a motive, and the suspect has not been named.

InXile is the studio behind the Wasteland series, and is currently working on Clockwork Revolution.

Knights of the Old Republic is my favorite RPG of all time, and a key reason why my love of video games developed as deeply as it did. My hopes for Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic, a spiritual successor to BioWare's classic, are sky-high, and expectations from the broader community are similarly intense. Director Casey Hudson isn't too worried about that pressure, though – after all, he and much of the team at Arcanaut Studios made the original KOTOR and the Mass Effect trilogy.

"I think it would be really weird to do if I hadn't worked on the first one," Hudson admits in an interview for The Fourth Curtain podcast. "It would feel really strange. But I think, for us, we've got folks on the team who worked on that game and have worked on all the Mass Effect games since and other BioWare stuff."

Hudson says that experience "helps," because the studio knows "why we did things the way we did. We're not trying to fill someone else's shoes, despite the expectations being really high."

We still know very little about Fate of the Old Republic, other than the fact that it's a spiritual successor to KOTOR. What kind of gameplay systems will it build on? I can't imagine KOTOR's creaky D&D 3.5-based mechanics are going to make a comeback. What kind of story will it tell? It's going to have to be something all-new, with the entire Star Wars universe having been rebooted since KOTOR was new.

"The thing that supersedes everything is our passion and excitement for doing something amazing," Hudson says. "That has to outshine everything else, because you can't really know how to answer pressure, and it's hard to even really understand what other people want to play. But if you're so excited about making something that people are going to love, you're just passionate about it being amazing, that leads you to where you want to go."

That's maybe an obvious answer, but I appreciate that it's the one Hudson is providing. No new game can possibly live up to my nostalgic memories of BioWare's Star Wars RPG, and what I really want is a new game created by a team of people who are excited about what they're making. If it can tap into my old love for KOTOR, that's just icing on the cake.

#3903. Guarding Stars Made A Major Change To The Book's Ending I Don't Understand

Spoilers for the movie Guarding Stars and the book The Bodyguard are ahead! You can stream the film with a Netflix subscription.

I try really hard not to judge a movie or TV show based on its source material and the changes made to it. In fact, I usually love it when a book-to-screen adaptation makes bold updates and takes creative liberties. However, when I watched Netflix’s Guarding Stars, which is based on Katherine Center’s novel, The Bodyguard, I couldn’t help but be baffled by a massive change that was made to the ending.

Alright, let’s get into the endings of these two projects that follow actor Jack Stapleton and his bodyguard, Hannah Brooks – who are played by CW icons Jared Padalecki and Leighton Meester, respectively, in the film – as they go from fake-dating to real love.

In Center’s book, The Bodyguard, after all covers are blown and everyone thinks Jack is safe, he's taken hostage. When Hannah shows up for a date with him, Jack tells her to go away in an effort to keep her safe. Ultimately, she realizes Jack didn’t mean what he said, and that he was in danger. So, she ran back into his home to save him, and to make a long story short, after a fight and a gunshot wound for Hannah, they survived and lived happily ever after.

In the movie on the 2026 Christmas schedule, nearly the same thing happens, except one vital change is made: Jack goes to Hannah’s apartment in New York to confess his love. When he gets there, she tells him she has company and does not share his feelings. Once he leaves, he realizes she was lying and goes back to save her. Ultimately, a similar kind of struggle plays out, and Hannah and Jack make it through safe and only slightly scathed, with Jack taking the gunshot wound instead of Hannah.

On the whole, this movie is very different from its source material. While it keeps the essence intact, a lot of the key elements of the novel are totally changed. However, this final sequence where Jack/Hannah gets taken hostage stays fairly similar; the film just switches who shows up and decides to save whom and who gets shot. So, why change it in the first place?

In the book, I loved that Hannah showed up to Jack’s house and saved him. It really showed off both how good she is at her job and how much she genuinely cares for the actor she was protecting. I also appreciated how that scene addressed her doubt about their relationship and made her realize that Jack really does love her.

In the movie, because Jack is the one who shows up for Hannah, we don’t fully get all of that. However, we do get to see him be a more active participant in this whole fiasco. While she still ultimately saves him in this big mess, it starts with him trying to protect her. To an extent, I get it, because Jack is more involved in the fight. However, what I loved about the book was that Hannah used this situation as the moment where she finally realized their shared feelings and got to kick butt in the process. I wish that's what had happened in the movie.

So, ultimately, while most of the changes in Guarding Stars didn’t bother me at all, this one did a bit. I just can’t understand why they’d swap the genders and have Jack go to save Hannah and keep the rest of the squirmish pretty much the same. However, it’s still a project on the 2026 movie schedule that’s worth a watch, and maybe a debate if you’ve also read the book.

#3902. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

While following a peculiar trail of silver and saffron leaves around the largest roots of the Treehouse, you come across a hexagonal wooden door lying half-hidden among ivy and moss. Scraping away the dirt, you discover a faint, absurd engraving of a newspaper. What mystery is here? You turn the brass knob – strange, it is warm! – and the engraving of the newspaper flutters. The pages turn faster and faster, emitting a howling gale that bowls you head over foot. When you pick yourself up, you are inside a vast attic full of books and bricabrac, lit from one side by windows that offer no view of the outside world – just light and mist.

Tarnation! You have been lured into the eternal prison of Sunday Afternoon. Fortunately, there are several ways to escape. Each of the arcane objects before you is secretly a portal, transporting you to another site of arcane activity, in a bizarre web of diversions that cannot possibly reflect the hand of a human curator. Which will you choose?

As you step forward, your toe nudges an ornamental scroll. It growls and wriggles like a panicking caterpillar, scooting away under a table. Before you lose sight of it, you discern the title and subject of the text – it's an essay by Kyle Tam about the yokai of Promise Mascot Agency.

Deep in a drawer, you discover a sour-smelling binder full of extracts from an ancient and all but indecipherable dispute over the discovery of "generative AI" in something called "Big Walk". The stakes are long-buried, but many of the individual pieces of writing are lively. Here is Bruno Dias noting in passing that "one of the harms of the 'AI' political project is the propaganda machine dedicated to making you feel stupid and helpless." Here is a professorial interjection from Brendan Keogh calling on the warring parties to recognise when "critiques of generative AI are actually just deflected critiques of the capitalist relations of technology and labour". Here is Mike Cook arguing that "what's happening is not unusual, it's not extreme, it's not unfair and it's not a 'public flogging'." Here is a ticker tape message from Hannah Nicklin observing that "if your radical position doesn’t have room for transformation it will not be safe until it contains just you".

A footnote in the same dusty sheaf of papers points you towards another work from Mike Cook in a different drawer. This one consists of neon slides, slotted into an antique View-Master, and explores a comparison between procedural generation and street photography.

Peering at the weirdly white and opaque windowpanes, you realise there are intricate equations traced in the condensation. It appears to be a post-mortem for a "post-cosy" game called Danchi Days, in which developer Melos Han-Tani discusses wishlist conversion rates and the problem of not fitting neatly into any recognisable genre.

A snowglobe stands on a mantelpiece, the flakes still orbiting a miniature washtub as though the object had been recently shaken, even though the chamber has clearly been abandoned for decades. You put it to your ear, anticipating the faint jingle of Xmas bells. Instead, you are almost deafened by a screeching guitar chord. Here is Erin Keane to explain.

Next to the snowglobe on the mantelpiece, there's a souvenir shop conch shell, polished to a high sheen. You put that to your ear, hoping to catch the soothing shuffle of surf on shingle, and a disembodied voice tells you to piss off. Tim Sniffen has some thoughts about gentrification, and why only he should be allowed to do it.

Again, one of these mystic artefacts hides the key to your release from the suffocating stillness of Sunday Afternoon. Which will you choose? Or have you, perhaps, brought a sorcerous teleportation device of your own? Please share. Here is Joanna Newsom's Cosmia to help you think.

#3901. EA hires another former Call of Duty boss to take the lead on all Battlefield Studios' projects

EA has made some notable leadership changes within its studios group, and in who oversees the Battlefield franchise. Byron Beede, previously Battlefield's general manager, has been promoted to group general manager.

Beede announced the change on LinkedIn, saying that he now oversees EA's shooter and action-RPG portfolio, seemingly occupying the role of the late Vince Zampella.

In this stead, EA appointed Sam Cooper as Battlefield's new boss. Cooper, who also revealed his new job title on LinkedIn, previously had a stint at EA Sports, but he's mostly known for his work at Activision, where he spent the last five-ish years as Call of Duty's global product management and head of live service.

While this might seem like fairly unremarkable corporate news - executives move between rival companies all the time, after all - it reinforces a narrative that EA continues to keenly replicate Activision's Call of Duty model.

That particular push is years-old now, and it kicked off in 2021 when EA hired Byron Beede, former boss of all of Call of Duty at Activision, to lead the next evolution of Battlefield. So far, that decision has given us the very successful Battlefield 6 and its free-to-play, COD: Warzone-like battle royale mode Redsec.

To facilitate that, EA rearranged several of its studios to serve under one banner dubbed Battlefield Studios, replicating Activision's model of locking several teams around the world into developing and supporting a single game / franchise. Ripple Effect, Motive, the iconic Criterion and, of course, series creator DICE are all the Battlefield franchise's lead and support studios.

Many players argue - and I would agree - that Battlefield and Call of Duty games are more alike today than they've ever been. The user interface, the emphasis on limited-time events, the garish store cosmetics, the COD-like battle pass system - complete with a more expensive option, are all signs of that transition. And that is to say nothing of controversial changes to longstanding Battlefield tenets, such as the class system, intended to make Battlefield 6 appeal to a wider audience.

The effects of that leadership change likely won't materialise until the next Battlefield title, but it's a curious one to keep in mind as EA leans even harder into its biggest franchises following its $55bn private equity and Saudi Arabia's PIF-funded buyout.

#3900. "We've finally reached this milestone": Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP kicks off open beta after around six years preparing for cybermayhem

"Let's see how the project handles real player traffic"

After a couple of years of regular testing behind closed doors, Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta, giving anyone who fancies a bit of multi-merc action a chance to give it a go. Though, if you do, be prepared for bugs and crashes, as work on the mod is far from over with the release of this "true beta".

As shown off in the video above, CyberMP's not about being able to play through the base game's missions with friends, but rather cruise around Night City as a gang getting into races and PvP shootouts. In that regard, it seems more akin to GTA 4's online mode than GTA 5's, with classic improvised hijinks the main draw over being able to pull off gigs with a crew. Though, there do also look to be roleplaying servers which could scratch the itch of those more interested in pretending to be a merc than blowing up other people's rides.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders wrote on Discord. "Anyone can jump in and play now — no invites or applications needed. Fair warning: this is a true beta. Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers. We welcome everyone: regular players, future server admins, and those who just love breaking game mechanics."

"Right now, our absolute priority is stability and fixing crashes," they continued later in the post. "New features are planned, but we need to polish the foundation first. A huge thank you to everyone who has been with us since the early versions, helped with closed testing, and patiently waited. We've finally reached this milestone. Let's see how the project handles real player traffic!"

According to the modders, CyberMP's "client doesn't have a digital signature yet", which could cause antivirus software not to be a fan of it. They're also anticipating "problems with the anti‑cheat system", so it may be worth holding off on giving the mod a go if you're not keen on being trolled by someone with the sort of destructive power usually reserved for megacorps and AIs from beyond the blackwall in the Cyberpunkverse.

For info on how to get CyberMP up and running, as well as create a custom server dedicated to the likes of roleplay or races, head over to its website. As you might expect, the mod requires a legit copy of Cyberpunk bought on either Steam, GOG, or the Epic store.

The console release of GTA 6 is here, in case you hadn't noticed. And us PC gamers are desperate to get hold of a version of our own, particularly as modders say it'll be playable on god's own platform within a week. Be careful what you click on, though, as NordVPN's threat intelligence team has discovered a nasty-sounding scam package on the dark web.

The company has posted a warning on X of a "GTA 6 PC scam kit" doing the rounds on the more dubious parts of the internet, using a fake GTA 6 PC port as bait.

A “GTA 6 PC scam kit” — yours for just $200. That’s what our Threat Intelligence team found on the dark web: a crypto wallet drainer, a fake “GTA6 Keygen.exe” that steals accounts, a YouTube Shorts bot to spread it, and a hidden crypto miner. The bait? A fake “GTA 6 PC Port.” But GTA 6 is console-only — there's no PC version coming on launch day. If you see one, it’s a scam. If it doesn’t come from the creators, don't click it!November 19, 2026

The package is said to be for sale for $200, or twice what a single copy of Grand Theft Auto VI: Ultimate Edition costs at retail. Included is a crypto wallet drainer, a fake "GTA6 Keygen.exe," and a hidden crypto miner. There's also a YouTube Shorts bot within the package, designed to help it spread.

All of which sounds comprehensively designed to screw over PC gamers looking to get their hands on GTA 6 ahead of an official release.

Speaking to Tech Radar ahead of the games launch, NordVPN CTO Marijus Briedis said: "Someone has packaged the whole scam and is selling it to anyone with $200. You don’t need any technical skills anymore."

"People who play on PC have been waiting for news, and any link promising an early PC version will get clicks," says Briedis. "There is no PC version on November 19. If you see one, it's a scam."

NordVPN isn't the only security provider warning of GTA 6 scams. Malwarebytes has detailed a number of dodgy sites that supposedly offer access to the game, each using the hype as a lure to convince you to give away your details and funnel you into various schemes.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

All of which compels me to restate the facts: GTA 6 does not have a PC release at the time of writing. In fact, it's not even been announced by Rockstar at this point. The game is available in Xbox Series X/S and PlayStation 5 versions only, and while modders seem to be beavering away on an unofficial PC version based on a leaked Xbox build, it's not available yet.

Don't let yourself be fooled into clicking shady links—and if you don't have a console like my good self, be prepared to wait. May I suggest playing all the other excellent games in your Steam backlog instead? It's not like we're short of PC games in general, you know.

#3898. Umamusume: Pretty Derby parent company plans to release seven new games by 2030 as it boasts an "88 percent hit rate" on its mobile titles

Cyberagent - the parent company of Umamusume: Pretty Derby developer Cygames - has boasted its recent successes in the mobile gaming sphere in a recent quarterly earnings presentation.

As part of this presentation (covered by Automaton), the company has established plans to launch seven "major releases" to the mobile platform by 2030. There is no word on what these games will be, but one will be released in 2027, while another two will come in 2028.

Cyberagent boasted an 88 percent "hit" rate for its mobile releases so far, with seven of its eight releases having a development budget of around a billion yen, and reaching a point where it makes that figure back every month from its playerbases. Those games include Umamusume: Pretty Derby, Final Fantasy Ever Crisis, Hololive Dreams, and Jujutsu Kaisen Phantom Parade.

CyberAgent CEO Takahiro Yamauchi - speaking during the presentation - noted that it was still difficult to predict the success of a mobile game ahead of its release. However, he also claims that the experience Cyberagent has gained with its big releases to date have allowed the company to gain a clearer perspective on profitability and sustainability.

This presentation comes after a notable month for Cygmes and Umamusume: Pretty Derby. The developer issued refunds for hotels and flights following the sudden cancellation of an LA live show for the game last month, then shortly after became a major sponsor of the Japanese Formula 1 Grand Prix. The game was also temporarily taken offline due to the major PHP vulnerability exposed last month, an outage that was thankfully short-lived.

#3896. "Nobody was hurt" in shooting near Clockwork Revolution devs InXile Entertainment's office, the Xbox-owned studio and police confirm

"Nobody was hurt" in a shooting last week near the California office of Clockwork Revolution developers InXile, both the studio and local police have confirmed. The incident, which took place on November 11th, is currently being investigated and police have reportedly taken a suspect into custody.

"Officers got there [on November 11th]," Tustin police sergeant Christopher Peterson said in statement to Aftermath. "They responded to a report of a drive-by shooting there. Located multiple shell casings. Nobody was hurt. Processed the crime scene, and then sometime [Friday] morning, a little before 11 [AM], they took a suspect into custody. And the investigation is still kind of ongoing as to where and why."

"We’re relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," a spokesperson for InXile said in a separate statement. "Our focus is on supporting our team, and we are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate."

InXile are set to release steampunk RPG Clockwork Revolution next year. The studio, developers of the likes of Wasteland 3 and The Bard's Tale IV, are one of the few Xbox-owned studios not to have been affected - at least as of writing - by Microsoft's ongoing mass layoffs this year.

Since being announced in 2023, Clockwork Revolution's dripped with Bioshock-ish vibes and popped up semi-regularly at Xbox showcases. "Wield the power of an incredible device to travel back in time, changing the past and rewriting the future of the city you call home: the vibrant steampunk metropolis of Avalon," reads its Steam synopsis. "In this immersive RPG, you'll step into the shoes of Morgan Vanette, a fully customizable player-character and member of the Rotten Row Hooligans. Travel between past and present as you battle the ruthless Lady Ironwood, who has been manipulating time to keep the working class struggling while amassing immense wealth and power."

Best wishes to the staff at InXile, here's hoping that going forwards they're able to get with making what's looking to be an intriguingly funky game without enduring any more concerning incidents like this one.

For years, Leroy Jethro Gibbs was the face of NCIS. His litany of rules and quirks was the heart and soul of the series, with his trademark head slap being one of them. As he's back in primetime on the Origins spinoff, I'm learning the slap all started with his former co-star, Michael Weatherly.

Mark Harmon spoke on its origins in an interview with Cheat Sheet, and how a bit of improvisation became an iconic recurring bit. Harmon set the scene far back before the 2026 TV schedule, all the way back to the first year of the series:

Michael is a hugely talented actor, as is every member of this cast. My memory of when that happened, we were doing a scene. And he was on a Navy ship and he was talking to a female petty officer. I think this was in year one, early. And he was doing what he does, which is sometimes stay on script and sometimes not. I just reached over and smacked him. I tried to put him back on line. It was an instinct. It wasn’t thought, I didn’t think about it, I just did it.

Funny to think this all started partly because Mark Harmon was frustrated with Michael Weatherly going off script. I could imagine filming days were long enough without improvisation that it could sabotage a scene that was perfectly written as-is. I can empathize with Harmon just wanting to move on, and giving Weatherly a smack on the head to remind him that other people would like to move on as well.

In fairness to Weatherly, Harmon's head slap could've caused a much bigger distraction had he completely broken character and gotten into a fight with his co-star. Fortunately, Harmon confirmed the Tony DiNozzo actor didn't miss a beat, and it became a part of the show's history:

To his credit, he stayed in the scene; he didn’t break. And I didn’t break. And the girl in the scene playing the petty officer, she was shocked, she was surprised. And she stayed there, and we just kept going. And people liked it. And every episode I was smacking him–maybe too much. We still do that occasionally, but sparingly. That’s where it came from.

It may not be the sole reason that NCIS is now a franchise generating billions of dollars across its lifetime, but it certainly contributed. Tony and Gibbs' relationship was one of the show's best parts in its early years, and many still remember it fondly.

What's funny about this story is that Michael Weatherly largely remembers it the same way, but added on detail that Harmon left out. In the moment, no one knew that the head smack was going to be something iconic in NCIS. It was only Season 1, and they were just a few episodes in.

Instead, Weatherly only remembers that he was goofing off, and everyone on set was mad at him afterward for potentially ruining a shot. It wasn't until they saw the head smack in the editing room that producers liked it and decided to make it a part of the episode and the show.

These days, Weatherly's Tony doesn't get a ton of head smacks. He's currently the acting director of the NCIS team, and also occasionally jumping in to lend a hand in investigations. I don't imagine anyone wants to slap the boss man on the back of the head, but I'd be up for seeing someone try.

NCIS continues on CBS on Tuesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. The entire evening is silly with spinoffs for the crime procedural, so anyone who isn't currently already aware of that should check it out!

#3894. The next Xbox, Project Helix, is a console and "not a PC" says Microsoft, as it clarifies that computational power isn't sole focus this time

"It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering."

Microsoft has stressed that its next-generation Xbox console, Project Helix, "is not a PC that can also play console games", but rather "a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC". The company has also underlined the importance of using gen-AI-adjacent "neural rendering" technology going forwards, and a desire to remove "all the barriers of play that have historically existed" - notably in making the past generations of games playable.

The details come from a Microsoft-produced Xbox magazine made available digitally yesterday, and a Helix-related feature speaking to Xbox vice president of next generation, Jason Ronald. "When we think about Project Helix, it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine," Ronald said, "one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed. My entire library is accessible to me. I'm able to bring four generations of my Xbox library and progression with me and have it available instantly. And we remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games.

"We're very clear on the design goal," Ronald later added. "Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customisability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."

Notably, Ronald seemed to suggest that Helix - the console, not the handheld; "Helix" refers to a couple of machines - isn't solely focused on computational grunt. Indeed, he said the next generation wasn't about hitting 8K resolutions and 240 hertz frame-rates, but instead leaning on technologies like "neural rendering" - i.e. generative-AI - and encouraging innovation.

"It's about deeper immersion," Ronald said. "It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering to deliver a new level of visual fidelity in more efficient and innovative ways. It's about new kinds of games and new game experiences that we haven't been able to do before. What excites me about the future is the idea of entirely new types of games that have never been possible before, delivered through all the innovation in the silicon and the hardware and the platform that we're delivering."

While referencing the global component shortage and exorbitant prices of computer hardware, he added: "This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that. I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last 10 years."

Xbox boss Asha Sharma also recently talked up the importance of generative-AI-sounding technology in Xbox's future, saying "too many ideas never become games", and that "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations".

Another key part of Xbox's Helix vision is compatibility and game preservation. "Game preservation is core to Xbox," Ronald went as far as to say. "Not only do we feel like it's the right thing for the industry, we feel a deep responsibility as one of its biggest platforms and publishers. For the first 30 years of game development, nobody really thought about game preservation when they were designing their hardware, when they were building their games." Xbox is apparently working with game-makers to ensure games can not only be played now but also 20 to 30 years into the future.

The other key facet of Microsoft's push the familiar Play Anywhere mantra, whereby one game can be played across multiple devices, maintaining your game-progress as you go. This is fundamental to Microsoft's handheld-and-console Helix plan, and something we've seen the company dry-run with the Xbox ROG Ally X handheld. "It's this notion that not only does my library move with me, but my progress moves with me as well," Ronald said. "Because I fully expect that when I'm in the middle of an 80-hour RPG, if I'm 25 hours into that and I want to play it on another device, I should be able to instantly resume from where I was. Those are things that today are becoming more common, but I think in the future it's going to be a baseline expectation of all players."

Ronald wouldn't be drawn on the issue of price regarding Project Helix - a recent report suggested Helix could be priced up to $1800 - referring to it only as both "a challenging time" but an "exciting one", because "we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also continuing to make things accessible and affordable". Ronald also wouldn't reference a release date, though the report referenced above suggested the handheld Helix machine will release next holiday, 2027, and the console Helix machine the year after. The next generation, then, seems to be around the corner.

#3892. Can GTA 6 make $2 billion in its opening weekend? One industry analyst has run the numbers, and seems to think so

We all know the story of GTA 5 making more than $1 billion in the first three days it was on sale, right? At the time, Take-Two believed this to be the fastest any entertainment property had achieved the impressive milestone - music and films included. It made history, and with ease. And it looks like GTA 6 is going to do even better.

At least, that's according to one analyst, Joost van Dreunen, a senior data analyst and great writer/numbers diviner who wrote some predictions in his respected SuperJoost PlayList newsletter. "My prediction: Take-Two announces opening-weekend sales above $2 billion by Monday, 23rd November," he wrote. And you know what? I reckon he's onto something.

Let's review what we already know: there is a conservative estimate of 10 million pre-orders for Rockstar's latest game floating around - something buoyed by comments from Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick - and, even by the company's lofty expectations, we know the game is tracking "well above expectations" when it comes to pre-orders.

We also know a lot of people are shelling out for the slightly more pricey Ultimate Edition (£90). So many people are opting for the more expensive version, in fact, that Take-Two revised its financial forecast up to $3.5bn for the next financial quarter, thanks to "recurrent consumer spending" (something Zelnick clarified in an investor's call is explicitly linked to the Ultimate Edition). 10 million pre-orders, at roughly $100 per copy - that's $1 billion right off the bat.

"That’s two days faster than its predecessor," van Dreunen said, "and largely before anyone has even played the game." That other $1bn will come over the weekend. And then, per the analyst, the game will sell roughly another 28 million copies over the course of the first year it's on sale. "My forecast puts first-year sales at 38 million copies, only modestly ahead of GTA 5’s 35 million. The real difference may be how much revenue each player generates over the years that follow."

But it's what follows in the newsletter that intrigues me most. "At the high end, [GTA 6] may just lift the entire industry with it," wrote van Dreunen. "In the face of AI slop and shitty mobile games that exist only to extract revenue, it will offer a reprieve. At a time when the industry is increasingly focused on making games cheaper and monetising players more aggressively, Rockstar is about to demonstrate the enduring appeal of spending a fortune to make something people actually want to play."

So, even if you're dubious about the game and Rockstar's motivations for selling as many copies as possible, the launch of GTA 6 could be something that gives the industry a much-needed jolt of life, in the face of rampant layoffs and shrinking talent pools.

It's not all sunshine and rainbows ahead for Rockstar, though: amongst the frenzy of launch activity, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

Back in 2021—which feels like an age ago now—Rockstar added a weird picture to a house in San Andreas in its Grand Theft Auto: The Trilogy—The Definitive Edition. It captured a small UFO hovering over a cream coloured bungalow with two palm trees in its front garden. It stood out because unlike some of the other pictures, players weren't really sure where it came from, but now we have an answer: It came from the future—bet you didn't see that one coming.

Well, actually some people did see it coming as they took it to be a tiny easter egg for a future GTA's Florida-setting, which we now know is correct. The picture wasn't just hinting at the location of Grand Theft Auto 6, though, it actually depicts a real location that players can go visit.

I saw this thanks to xGarbett's easter egg video, but quickly sent our own Mollie Taylor after the scent. After driving around Belville for a little while we found it: the UFO house. Mystery solved—or was it? Well as it turns out you can go into this house during the day and inside is yet another mystery.

Walking into the garage of this home, players will be met by a sprawling mind map plastered across the wall with "IT'S A SIMULATION" written in big red letters in the middle. Oh dear, an NPC has gained sentience.

There are other phrases across the cork board such as:

I'm no psychologist, but this may be an issue.

We didn't encounter the owner of this house, luckily, but there were brochures scattered around about a boat. Seems like he's going to try and head for the open ocean in a bid to break through the map and finally gain freedom. Good luck buddy, I wish you well. Hopefully, if it all goes sideways out there the jetski dog will help him out—that'll probably make it on the conspiracy dream board.

#3890. GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty to 2022 Rockstar Games breach which the company claim cost them $5 million

Hacker was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

Kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the company contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent company Take-Two quickly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

Hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely shows anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

#3889. Ever wanted to play a multiplayer version of Cyberpunk 2077 with your friends? Well, thanks to a mod now in beta, you can

You may have recently read that CD Projekt Red's in-development Cyberpunk 2 may be trying to revive the original game's online ambitions. But, if you don't want to wait the many years it'll likely be before the Cyberpunk 2077 sequel arrives, then I've got good news for you: Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders on the CyberMP Discord channel wrote (thanks RPS). "Anyone can jump in and play now - no invites or applications needed." The team notes, however, that this is "true beta", meaning "Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers."

Alongside the potential shakiness, the devs say it's also possible the mod could ping your anti-virus software, since it "doesn't have a digital signature yet". Whilst the priorities for the team lie in "polishing the foundations" and "fixing crashes and stability", more features are eventually planned. But for now, they stress, "let's see how the project handles real player traffic!"

So, what exactly is it? CyberMP is a dedicated multiplayer modification for Cyberpunk 2077 that allows you and your friends to explore Night City together: drive vehicles, engage in combat, and play custom community-created game modes on high-tick dedicated servers. You need an official copy of the game to play it (obviously), and the mod is completely free to download. You can download the mod, and read a fair amount of how to get it working, what to expect from it, and how to troubleshoot any issues, over at its dedicated website.

If you're thinking 'Hang on, why does Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer sound so familiar?', it's because the game was supposed to receive an official multiplayer mode after its original release. Thanks to its shaky launch, however, plans changed, and CD Projekt Red later announced that multiplayer would be a separate "triple-A release", but, eventually, that too was cancelled. The studio is still keen to honour the idea, though, and recently stated it's "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day".

This isn't the first big bit of news we've had about Cyberpunk 2077 mods this week. Just yesterday, a new mod called 'Torrent' added 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City - all rendered and made lovely with a new lighting system that seems to play nicely with other weather mods that have been created for the game.

The Hunger Games is a bonafide shared universe.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spoilers ahead for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

The Hunger Games movies have entertained audiences for decades now, and we're getting yet another book to screen adaptation with Francis Lawrence's Sunrise on the Reaping. The latest prequel tells the story of Haymitch's games, with actor Joseph Zada perfectly emulating Woody Harrelson. There are still some surprises for those who read the book, including a few references to Lucy Gray from Songbirds and Snakes (which is streaming with a Hulu subscription) that weren't in the source material. CinemaBlend spoke to the movie's director about why those changes were made for the latest installment in the franchise.

Years after the original Hunger Games movies, we've returned to Panem thanks to author Suzanne Collins' pair of prequels. First was Songbirds and Snakes, which followed a young President Snow who fell in love with and then lost Rachel Zegler's Lucy Gray Baird. Lucy Gray's fate is left ambiguous in both the film and book, as she disappeared and fled from Snow after winning the 10th Hunger Games.

Sunrise on the Reaping's movie deviates from the book by having Snow mention Lucy Gray by name when talking to Haymitch at Plutarch's home. As you can see in the video above, I had to ask Francis Lawrence about this change, and he told me:

That's not in the book. And that came out of conversations that we had with Suzanne and our screenwriter when we're going through and just talking about, you know, you have to go into every scene and go 'How? Why?' all of that. And we started to question about Snow making this appearance and why him coming in person is so important, especially when he's, you know, not feeling so well. Not to spoil anything. And that's what we came up with, which I was really happy about is this idea of this kind of personal quest that for 40 years he's still been obsessed with what happened to Lucy Gray.

Honestly, this makes a great deal of sense. While Haymitch makes a quick enemy out of Snow during the Chariot sequence that killed Louella, why would the President of Panem (played in this film by Ralph Fiennes) show up in person to intimidate him? This scene was expanded in the film by having Snow specifically talk about Lucy Gray, the District 12 victor and his love interest that he's still seemingly searching for. Whether or not we ever get confirmation about her ultimate fate remains to be seen.

In addition to Snow name-dropping Lucy Gray, we also get another reference to Zegler's character during the funeral scene towards the end of the movie. At the services for the District 12 tributes like Maysilee, the Covey sing "The Old Therebefore," the song Lucy Gray belts out as snakes cover her body at the end of her Games. In our same conversation Lawrence explained how this came about, telling me:

Suzanne is a real music aficionado. And, you know, she obviously was very involved in writing many lyrics for the previous songs and all of that. And has, you know, sort of her mythology of how these songs have been sung and what songs have been passed along. That was one of the ideas too, is that that's the kind of song that you would sing at a funeral, which is partially why Lucy Gray sings it when she thinks that she's gonna die, so that she's almost singing her own funeral song. So, but it's just nice that you, you feel those kind of connections, and it's the same with The Hanging Tree, you hear Lucy Gray singing that, but you've already heard Katniss singing it.

I honestly love this attention to detail. While these are not huge moments in the Hunger Games movies, the way songs are used throughout the franchise helps to make the cinematic universe feel more interconnected. There's a ton of lore within the story of Panem, and these small changes to Sunrise on the Reaping will no doubt be powerful for longtime fans of the YA franchise.

Francis Lawrence mentioned this being a goal in including "The Old Therebefore" in the newest Hunger Games movie, saying:

But that's just a song that she's heard and has been passed down for years, you know, in District 12. So it's just, it's nice how everything interconnects.

Sunrise on the Reaping's reviews have been mixed, but now moviegoing audiences will get to judge the latest Hunger Games flick for themselves. Fans are hoping to see more prequels in the future, but that'll presumably only happen once Suzanne Collins release another novel. Fingers crossed that happens sooner rather than later.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list. Fingers crossed that the franchise keeps expanding with more prequels.

You could risk a ban by auto-uploading GTA 6 clips to the Xbox Network

If you're playing GTA 6 on Xbox, you should turn off your console's automatic upload feature or you could risk having your Xbox account suspended. An Xbox user on Reddit reported receiving a two-day, unrepealable ban for automatically uploading a 28-second clip of GTA 6 characters at the beach. According to the Reddit user, sangobar, the clip was almost immediately flagged by the Xbox Network for either violating the Xbox Community Standards or Microsoft Services Agreement terms (the email they received from Xbox doesn't specify which). However, the user claims the clip only showed characters in beachwear and the clip was therefore incorrectly flagged.So, to avoid the risk of an Xbox ban it is better to be safe than sorry, to disable your Xbox automatic upload feature, and to understand what Xbox's guidelines are around the content you can upload to the Xbox Network.

Automatic uploads to the Xbox Network are enabled as standard on Xbox, meaning the GTA 6 clips you capture on your console are automatically uploaded to the Xbox Network. To turn off your Xbox Series X's automatic uploads feature, follow these steps:

One Drive is more lenient in what you can upload, but if you'd rather not automatically upload any of your GTA 6 capture, it's best to set both it and Xbox Network to 'Don't Upload'.

GTA 6 clips could potentially violate the 'Keep your content clean' term of the Xbox Community Standards, specifically the 'Make stuff that's suitable for all audiences rule', which states: "The Xbox community must be friendly and accessible to everyone, this isn't the appropriate place for sexual content. Keep your public posts and messages suitable for all ages and audiences."

According to Xbox, some examples of content that could violate this term include sharing or distributing non-consensual intimate imagery, links or imagery that displays pornography, screenshots or game clips that include mature sexual content, custom gamerpics that contains nudity, lewd messages to other players, and distasteful or inappropriate pictures. In other words, be careful before sharing images or clips of GTA 6's more mature content, like GTA 6 strip clubs.

#3886. Intel are being sued for "misleading" investors about "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory" thanks to AI-fuelled price hikes

Tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they announced a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

The lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year.

The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen".

They also accuse the company of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above."

Finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Company chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales."

Once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. As regards graphics cards, they have long been dwarfed by Nvidia.

Any Intel investor who wants a piece of that lawsuit has until January 12th 2027 to sign up as a lead plaintiff – that is, a court appointee who represents the interests of other class members. As regards us little people who don't buy stock in huge technology corporations, all this merely continues the weird existential crisis wrought upon 'traditional' gaming and computing hardware by the feckless quest to sell a better chatbot.

#3885. World of Warcraft: Forever completionists push back as Blizzard gives them a powerful toy and then prepares to take it away

"Exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors."

With the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever there's a whole new world filled with niche gear and strange baubles to collect. But one item in particular has drawn the ire of the creators of a popular completionist add-on.

That add-on is All the Things, a must-install for collectors like me, as it acts as a database of all the gear, mounts, titles, crafting recipes, and super rare drops in the game. Once you collect something, it is hidden in the add-on, thus tracking your progress and making for a fantastic tool for picking the game apart.

On occasion, specific items have written notes attached by the All the Things development team, as is true of a special World of Warcraft: Forever toy, the Pouch of Violet Dust. This is a promotional item that was obtainable by watching two hours of WoW Forever streams between the 4th and 12th November.

It's a powerful toy! When used on a campfire, it changes the fire's colour to purple and extends the buffs provided by it from the usual one hour to two hours. But the sticking point with the item isn't its existence, rather the fact that it's going to be removed in early December, not long from now.

This is what the creators of the All the Things add-on don't like. "A week-long, Twitch-only window for an item that gets taken away a month later is exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors," the creators said in a note attached to the item in the mod. "It can't be earned by playing the game at all. Even those who get it don't get to keep it."

They aren't alone in feeling this way. Comments below the item's listing on the Wowhead database are equally scorching. "I love FOMO in their explicitly non-fomo game," wrote user TheWhiteRose.

"Just... Why?" added user Darrenic427. "They could very easily just patch out the camp buff duration and keep the visual effect, but Blizzard just doesn't like pretty fire I guess. Figures that they finally give us access to purple fire but then take it away after a month."

The battle between collectors and time-limited FOMO items is one that has been waged for about as long as these sorts of items have been a part of games. Though for the pouch, it's an especially weird case: an item that's cool to have but so temporary in nature that it makes it both important to completionists and strangely pointless to care about. Whether it makes a return in a later update for World of Warcraft: Forever and doesn't require out-of-game actions to obtain, and doesn't disappear, we'll have to wait and see.

WoW Forever itself is proving popular among players - me included. It's added a staggering amount of new quests and many new features to the original version of World of Warcraft, which, in turn, has injected the game with an impressive amount of new items to collect. Completionists will likely be glued to the game for a long time.

#3883. Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be announced, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a new GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

The influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

The city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

Much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

The Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on New Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. But I'm even more pleased that as the studio's aged, their work has grown closer to Illusion Softworks'.

#3882. UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is more worried "about the amount of time" people will spend on GTA 6 than the game's violent content

"I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games."

Leader of the UK Conservative Party (and former Mortal Kombat player) Kemi Badenoch is more worried about the amount of time people will spend playing GTA 6 rather than the game itself.

Every new Grand Theft Auto game invites some amount of controversy over its in-game violence or depictions of sex and drugs - from San Andreas' raunchy Hot Coffee mini-game to GTA 5's graphic torture scene. Ahead of GTA 6's release this week, the Tory leader downplayed those fears.

"I would be more worried about the amount of time people were spending on a game than the game specifically. I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games," Badenoch said in a news conference shared by Sky News (good spot, IGN).

While Badenoch's stance might be surprising for the normally right-wing UK political party, she did still worry over children who might play GTA 6 for too long. There are probably far worse ways for kids to spend their time than engaging with a long-form story like GTA 6's, though, especially in an era with endless amounts of 10-second clips to mindlessly scroll past and declining funding into youth programs.

"I haven't played Grand Theft Auto, I know people are worried about the game content. At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half an hour on it and then went out and did something else. They are two different things," Badenoch added.

GTA 6's release is imminent and is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. One analyst even suggested GTA 6 could make over $2bn in its opening weekend - that's handily more money than Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey made during its entire run in cinemas, for context.

If you'd like to reminisce a bit before the long-awaited game finally hits, you can check out our favourite Grand Theft Auto pieces Eurogamer's published over the years.

Spoilers ahead for The Traitors: New Blood Finale.

In just a few short years The Traitors has become one of my favorite shows on television. The Emmy-winning competition series just had its first season with non-celebrities called New Blood, which aired on NBC (and streaming with a Peacock subscription). While fans have criticism for New Blood as a whole, I thought the two-episode finale was a thrilling conclusion. And I can't stop thinking about how the losers reacted to the news at the final Fire of Truth ceremony. Let's break it all down.

I'm counting the days for the next celebrity-filled Traitors cast to get on my TV, but New Blood was a fun watch that really stuck the landing with its finale. At the Fire of Truth ceremony sweaty boy Victor and Traitor Katie were voted off, leaving just Wyatt, Abbey, and Shane in host Alan Cumming's castle. The latter was recruited via an ultimatum a few episodes ago, meaning he got to take home the full $246,300 prize pot.

Wyatt and Abbey were completely blindsided by this, and clearly had whiplash from thinking they won the money to realize they'd bee duped. They both cried in response, reminding me of Cirie's win back in Season 1. But after asking some follow up questions, and seeing Shane's tear-filled reaction to cheating his friends, the two Faithful sucked it up, walked over to him and hugged the season's winner.

While it took until the reunion for Andie to forgive Cirie back in Season 1, I was so impressed by the way that Abbey and Wyatt were able to put their hurt feelings aside and give Shane the support he needed in this emotional moment. I truly can't stop thinking about the two of them walking over to him from opposite sides of the Round Table, and embracing him as he cried.

The high emotions for New Blood make more sense than the celebrity seasons, as the prize pot is more a life-changing sum of money for civilians. So I would have understood if grudges were formed, especially by Abbey and Wyatt. As such, it's doubly impressive that wasn't the case, and they were able to support and forgive Shane.

This sentiment of sportsmanship continued during the final moments of The Traitors: New Blood's finale, where all five of the finalists celebrated Shane's victory with champagne and fireworks outside the castle. While fruit gate was previously my favorite episode, I've got to say that this finale took the cake.

The Traitors: New Blood is streaming in its entirety on Peacock as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Now we just have wait a few months until the next celebrity season premiers on the streaming service.
